migrationNotes: Spine: a form asks for ages and one answer is the word 'unknown'. The lesson catches that failure on purpose (try/except ValueError), chooses between a fallback and a skip, counts and reports what was skipped, then follows the answers into a file (with closes it, blank lines need a policy) and finally asks which file a relative name means (working directory).
Left out of the lesson (still in the course): python-errors-and-resources-hook (the mean of 24 and 36, covered by the opener).
Figures: the try/except and rejected-counter figures moved onto the teaching screens that explain them.

lesson.title: Handle failure without hiding it

lead.text: Turning text into a number is the step where the form goes wrong. int('18') gives the number 18. int('unknown') cannot work, so Python raises a ValueError. An error raised like this is called an exception, and unless something deals with it the program stops. Python lets you deal with it. The risky line goes under try:, and under except ValueError: you say what to do if that exception occurs. If the conversion works, the except lines are skipped. If it raises a ValueError, Python jumps to them and carries on afterwards.

Name the exception you expect. Writing except ValueError catches the failure you planned for and nothing else. A bare except would catch every mistake, even a misspelt variable name, which hides real bugs behind a quiet fallback. In the picture the fallback is 0. Step through an age of '18' and an age of 'unknown'.

afterFigure.text: With '18' the conversion succeeds and value is 18, so the except lines never run. With 'unknown' the conversion fails, the except lines run and value becomes 0. A fallback of 0 is a choice, and it is not always a good one. An age of 0 would drag an average down, which the next screens come back to.

lead.text: Decide what Python does with text that has no digits in it.
The except lines run only if the conversion fails. Decide whether it fails for this text.

What happens to the bad entry is your choice, and the choice changes the answer. One option is to substitute a fallback and carry on. That suits a count where a missing value really does mean none, such as a drink nobody sold. Inside a loop over the entries, the try line is total += int(text) and the except line is total += 10. A bad entry adds 10 to total in place of its own value, and the good ones add what they hold. With the entries '4', 'y' and '5', total ends at 19.

For ages the better option is to skip. A made-up age of 0 or 10 is a number nobody gave, and it pulls the average towards itself. Skipping leaves the entry out so that only real answers count. In code the except lines simply leave total alone, and with the same three entries total ends at 9. Either way the program carries on, which is the point of catching the exception. What remains to settle is how a reader can tell that entries were left out.

A total built from skipped data looks just like a total built from complete data, and a reader has no way to tell the difference. The remedy is to count what was left out. A second accumulator, rejected, starts at 0 and goes up by 1 inside the except lines. It counts the entries that failed while total adds up the ones that worked. Step through the picture, where each entry is a piece of text to be added.

afterFigure.text: With '2' and '5' both convert, total is 7 and rejected is 0. With '2', 'bad' and '5' the middle entry fails, total is still 7 and rejected is 1. The same total comes from different data, and only the count shows which case you are in. Reporting a share is clearer still. One rejected entry out of 4 is 25 per cent, which tells a reader how much of the data the total leaves out.

lead.text: Turn the count of rejected entries into a share of all the entries.

The answers usually live in a file, and reading a file brings its own problem. Opening a file ties up something the operating system hands out, and it has to be given back by closing the file. A program that stops half-way can leave it open. The with statement looks after this. with open('answers.txt') as f: opens the file, runs the indented lines and closes the file when they end, even if one of them fails. The object that does this work is called a context manager.

with looks after the file. It does nothing about what is inside. The lines come back as text, so every line still needs converting, and a blank line is an empty string that int cannot read. Decide how to treat blank lines before converting. The method strip removes spaces and the line break from the ends of a string, so line.strip() == '' picks out a blank line and lets you skip it. The rejected count can tell a reader how many there were.
Separate looking after the file from checking what is inside it.

steps.headline: Which file does a name mean

lead.text: Opening 'answers.txt' needs a path, the address of a file. A path with no folder in it, such as answers.txt or data.csv, is a relative path, and Python resolves it from the working directory, which is the folder the program was launched from. It is not the folder that holds the script. Launch the same script from a different folder and the same name can point at a different file, or at no file at all.

That explains a common puzzle. A script works in one terminal window and reports 'file not found' in another, with nothing changed in the code. Before blaming the file, check where Python started. A full path that begins at the top of the drive always names the same place, wherever the program is launched from.
The script is the same every time. Only the folder it is launched from changes.

lesson.orientation: Catch expected exceptions and manage files with a context manager.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: A form asked for age. Three people answered: 24, unknown and 36. Anyone working out the average age reads the three answers and sets the middle one aside without a second thought. The average of 24 and 36 is 30, and everyone agrees that unknown is not an age.

A program has no such instinct. Asked to turn each answer into a number, it reaches the word unknown and cannot read it as digits, so it stops with an error message. The work done so far is lost, and so is every answer after the bad one. A form with ten thousand rows will always have a few entries like that.

This lesson is about what a program should do instead. It looks at expecting a failure on purpose and at choosing what happens when one occurs. Then it covers how to report how much data was left out. The second half moves to the files such answers are stored in: how to read one without leaving it open, and how Python decides which file a name refers to.

intro.promise: By the end you'll catch an expected error on purpose and read a file inside a with block.

recap.keyIdea: Catch the specific error you expect and say what you skipped. A with block closes the file, and relative paths follow the working directory.

blocks.text: You averaged the two valid ages to get 30. You skipped 2 bad entries to reach a total of 10, and found that 3 of 5 entries, 60 per cent, were rejected. Three launch folders gave three different files, because a relative path follows the working directory.

recap.nextHook: The ages are clean now but they sit in a list, and a list is built to hold anything. Data work usually means thousands of values of one kind laid out in a grid, such as seats in a cinema or readings from a sensor. The next lesson introduces the NumPy array, which holds a grid of one kind of value and works on all of it at once.

questions.prompt: Parse '24' with int, using 0 only on ValueError. What value is produced?
hints: The exception branch runs only if conversion fails.
The input contains valid integer digits.
Use the converted value because no exception is raised.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The conversion succeeds, so the fallback is never used.

questions.onCorrect: 24. The conversion succeeded, so the except branch never ran.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the fallback. The conversion succeeded, so it is never used.

questions.prompt: What is the total of the entries that convert?
hints: Add only the successful conversions.
Mark each entry as converted or failed.
Add the values of the entries that converted.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The valid entries are 4 and 6, which sum to 10. Two entries were rejected.

questions.onCorrect: 10. Only 4 and 6 converted, so only they joined the total.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the first. The entry '6' converts too.
Two entries convert, so the total is not empty.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of with open(...) as f?
hints: Resource handling and data checking are separate jobs.

acceptedIdeas: It closes the file when the block exits
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The context manager closes the file when the block ends. Reading and validation can still fail.

choices.label: It closes the file when the block exits
It guarantees all file contents are valid

questions.onCorrect: It closes the file when the block exits. Reading and validating the contents are still your job.

misconceptions.feedback: with manages the file, not its contents. Bad text still raises errors.
Errors still happen. with only makes sure the file is closed afterwards.

questions.prompt: A script opens data.csv with no folder in the path. You launch it from three different folders, each holding its own data.csv. How many different files does it read?
hints: Where does Python look for a path with no folder?
It looks in the folder Python was launched from.
Each launch folder has its own file.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Relative paths resolve from the current working directory, so each launch reads its own file.

questions.onCorrect: 3. A relative path follows the working directory, so each launch folder gave a different file.

misconceptions.feedback: That assumes the path follows the script. A relative path follows the folder Python was launched from.

questions.prompt: How many entries fail int conversion in ['7', '8.5', 'no', '2']?
hints: int parses an integer string, not any numeric text.
Does int accept a string with a decimal point?
Check each entry and count only the failures.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: '8.5' is not an integer string, and 'no' is not numeric. The other two conversions succeed.

questions.onCorrect: 2. '8.5' is not an integer string and 'no' is not numeric. The other two convert.

misconceptions.feedback: Check '8.5': int does not accept a decimal point in its text.
The first and last entries are plain integer strings, so they convert.

questions.prompt: A file has lines 5, a blank line, and 9. You skip blank lines. What is the sum?
hints: Apply the blank-line policy before converting.
A line whose stripped content is empty is skipped.
Convert the remaining two lines and add them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The two retained numbers are 5 and 9, giving 14.

questions.onCorrect: 14. The blank line was skipped before conversion, so only 5 and 9 were added.

misconceptions.feedback: The 9 is a valid line. Only the blank is skipped.

hints: Which entries convert, and which raise ValueError?
The failing entry adds the fallback of 10.
Add the two converted values and the fallback.

questions.onCorrect: 13. 1 and 2 converted, and the except branch added 10 for 'x'.

misconceptions.feedback: That skips the fallback. The except branch adds 10 for the entry that failed.
That is only the fallback. The two valid entries are added too.

hints: Which answers are numbers?
Leave out the answer that is not a number.
Add the two ages and divide by 2.
questions.prompt: What is the mean age of the people who gave a number?
questions.onCorrect: 30. You set aside the answer that is not a number and averaged the rest. Code must make the same choice on purpose.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by 3. The unknown answer is not part of the average.
That is the sum of the ages. Divide by how many there are.

hints: Can the text seven be read as digits?

questions.onCorrect: It raises a ValueError. The text is not integer digits, and int refuses rather than guessing.

misconceptions.feedback: int never invents a fallback. You supply one with except.
int returns a number or raises an error. It does not hand text back.

choices.label: The reader learns how much data was left out
Python requires a counter for except

questions.onCorrect: The reader learns how much data was left out. Skipping silently hides a change to the data.

questions.prompt: Parse ['10', 'x', '20', 'y', 'z'] as integers, skipping ValueError entries. What percentage of entries were rejected?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 3 of 5 entries were rejected, which is 60 per cent.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share that converted. The question asks for the share rejected.
That is the count of rejected entries. Turn it into a percentage of all five.

with open(...) closes the file; it does not validate contents.
A relative path resolves from the working directory, the folder Python was launched from, not from the script's folder.
The same relative path reads a different file from each launch folder.
